evidence.says: Lists Paul Lachance's Imagery of Generations dissertation under European History for 1974–1975.
Lists Paul Lachance (1938–2011) and his 1984 book The Spiritual Journey of the Blessed Angela of Foligno.
Paul Lachance taught spiritual theology at Catholic Theological Union and studied Angela of Foligno.

basis: The sources identify a Wisconsin history dissertation and an Angela of Foligno scholar, but do not establish whether their authors were the same person. The different research and career information alone does not rule out one person with two careers.

evidence.says: The catalogue credits Saturday night forever to Alan Jones (Alan Stanley) and Jussi Kantonen.
The bibliography credits The equestrian motif in Coptic textiles (1974) to Alan Michael Jones and identifies it as a dissertation.
A citation identifies A. M. Jones's The Equestrian Motif in Coptic Textiles as a 1974 Wayne State University PhD dissertation.

basis: The works are attributed to Alan Stanley Jones and Alan Michael Jones, respectively. Their different recorded middle names support identifying them as different people, though the sources do not explicitly compare them.

evidence.says: The bibliography credits Thomas L. Burton with Experiments in Recreation Research (1971) and other recreation research titles.

basis: The recreation publications are documented, but I found no source connecting their author to the reviewer or establishing separate careers. The review itself could not be accessed to identify its author further.

evidence.says: Cristóbal Rovira Kaltwasser, Berlin, reviewed Bohlender's Metamorphosen des liberalen Regierungsdenkens in 2008.
Cristóbal Rovira Kaltwasser was a PhD student at Humboldt University of Berlin in 2004–2008 and a Sussex fellow from 2011.
His CV lists Populism in Europe and the Americas and the 2004 contribution Der Beitrag der Dependencia-Schule.

basis: The review names Berlin, where the scholar on the other key was a doctoral student at the time. The review does not identify an institution, and no source found connects it to that scholar's works, so the shared location and name are insufficient for a merge.

evidence.says: The publisher attributes a review of After Genocide to Stephanie Wolfe in H-Genocide.
Weber State lists Stephanie Wolfe's The Politics of Reparations and Apologies and In the Shadow of Genocide.

basis: The sources identify the review and the other works, but do not establish that their authors are the same person. The shared name and subject alone are insufficient to merge the keys.

evidence.says: The AHA lists Ira Leonard's New York City Politics, 1841-1844: Nativism and Reform at New York, February 1965.
Ira Leonard earned a Ph.D. and was a history professor at Southern Connecticut State University for nearly 40 years.

basis: The AHA identifies the dissertation author, and Southern describes a history professor with the same name, but the sources do not connect that dissertation or its university to the reviewer. The overlap in name and field is insufficient to establish identity.

evidence.says: The catalogue credits The Impact of the Telegraph on Contract Law (1990) to Lester G. Lindley.
The 2003 conference program lists Lester G. Lindley at Nova Southeastern University.

basis: The book author and the reviewer have the same full name, and a conference program places a person of that name at the reviewer's institution. I found no source connecting the book or dissertation to that affiliation or to the reviews, so the identity remains unconfirmed.

evidence.says: Cambridge lists Robert Shephard as the author of the 1991 review of The Gloucestershire Gentry.
A citation attributes Royal Favorites in the Political Discourse of Tudor and Stuart England, a 1985 Claremont PhD thesis, to R. P. Shepheard.

basis: The review and dissertation have compatible names and subjects, but the sources found do not connect the dissertation author to the reviewer or establish a shared institution at the relevant time.

evidence.says: Elizabeth Spencer authored the 2018 apron article; its author note says she had recently completed doctoral research at York.
Elizabeth Spencer earned a York BA in 2013 and MA in 2015; her undergraduate dissertation studied the apron.

basis: The apron author's 2013 BA and recent doctoral research place her academic career far too late to be the author of the 1933 Hakewill thesis recorded under the other key. The career distinction is inferred from the dates and identified works.

evidence.says: The author of Beauty Up earned a UCLA anthropology PhD in 1988 and joined UMSL in 2010.
UMass Amherst lists Laura Miller and All-American Vacationland among its 2014 history PhD recipients.
Miller's CV lists Beauty Up and a UMSL professorship from 2010 to 2017.

basis: The records describe different doctorates and careers: the Beauty Up author was a UMSL professor during the years of the UMass history doctorate. The separate institutional records strongly indicate two scholars.

evidence.says: Peter Wolf reviewed Ralf Pröve's Stadtgemeindlicher Republikanismus for H-Soz-u-Kult in January 2002.
The catalogue attributes The Future of the City: New Directions in Urban Planning (1974) to Peter M. Wolf.

basis: The review identifies its author only as Peter Wolf; the sources found do not connect him to Peter M. Wolf's books or establish a different career. The shared name and urban subject matter are insufficient to resolve the pair.

evidence.says: The 1973 dissertation The Evolution of Industrial Capitalism in Rhode Island is listed under James Lawson Conrad.
James L. Conrad Jr. is identified as a Nichols College history professor; his 1973 Connecticut dissertation is cited.
Rebel Reefers is by James Lee Conrad, identified as a colonel in the U.S. Air Force Advocate General's Department.

basis: The dissertation author is James Lawson Conrad, a Nichols College history professor, while the author of Rebel Reefers is James Lee Conrad, an Air Force legal officer. Their distinct full names and careers indicate two people.

evidence.says: Louisiana State University Press identifies Grace Porter Miller as the author of Call of Duty, published in 1999.
The references credit Grace Miller with a January 2021 H-Nationalism review of First Founding Father.

basis: The sources identify the authors of the two works, but no source found links the review to Grace Porter Miller or establishes that they are different people. The H-Net review page was inaccessible during this search.

evidence.says: Christoph Schank, Bergisch, reviewed Religion im Kaiserreich for H-Soz-Kult on 20 January 1998.
Christoph Schank wrote Kölsch-katholisch, published in 2004; the book is based on a dissertation accepted at the University of Cologne in 2002.
A 2007 conference lists Dr. Christoph Schank of Bergisch Gladbach speaking on the Catholic milieu in the Cologne parish of St. Agnes.

basis: The review and the book are attributed to Christoph Schank, and the review's abbreviated location and the later conference provide suggestive context. No source found connects the review to the book author or establishes the required institutional link in the relevant years.

evidence.says: Claudia Siebrecht reviewed the 2006 conference Crimes against Humanitarian Law at Trinity College Dublin; the report gives no author affiliation.
A review states that Claudia Siebrecht's The Aesthetics of Loss is based on her PhD thesis at Trinity College Dublin.
Trinity College Dublin lists Claudia Siebrecht's 2007 PhD thesis, Death, sacrifice and mourning in German women's art of the First World War.

basis: The conference report and the book author's doctorate both connect to Trinity College Dublin at similar dates. The report does not establish the reviewer's affiliation or otherwise link her to the book, so the evidence falls short of a decisive identity link.

evidence.says: Michiko Suzuki wrote Humanitarian Internationalism Under Empire, works at the University of Tokyo and received her doctorate at SOAS.
Michiko Suzuki of Indiana University reviewed Gender and Law in the Japanese Imperium in September 2015.
Michiko Suzuki previously worked at Indiana University, received a Stanford PhD and held an Indiana research award in 2015.
The 2024 conference program lists Michiko Suzuki of UC Davis and Michiko Suzuki of the University of Tokyo as separate participants.

basis: The book author and the UC Davis scholar are distinct people, as the conference program shows. The review's 2015 Indiana affiliation identifies the latter scholar by inference; she held an Indiana award that year, while the book author was pursuing research at SOAS.

evidence.says: University of Iowa Press names Chris Rasmussen as author of Carnival in the Countryside: The History of the Iowa State Fair, published in 2015.
A citation identifies Chris A. Rasmussen's State Fair: Culture and Agriculture in Iowa, 1854-1941 as a 1992 Rutgers PhD dissertation.

basis: The sources identify the book and dissertation on the second key, but I found no source connecting their author to the 1999 reviewer or the reviewer's institutional appointments. The shared name and compatible career dates do not establish identity.

evidence.says: The 2004 review of Isaak Dunaevskij is by Michael John, Lotman Institute for Russian and Soviet Culture, Ruhr University Bochum.
Michael John's profile lists Hausherrenmacht und Mieterelend (1982) and Wohnverhältnisse sozialer Unterschichten (1984), and an affiliation at the University of Linz.

basis: The review and the books are associated with different institutions, and no source found connects the reviewer to the book author. The affiliations alone do not establish that they are different people.

evidence.says: Céline Trautmann-Waller reviewed Was sind Kulturwissenschaften?: 13 Antworten in January 2006.
Céline Trautmann-Waller's publication list includes Aux origines d'une science allemande de la culture (2006).

basis: The review and the publication list share a name, but the sources found do not independently connect the review to the author of the book. The shared name and subject alone do not establish identity.

evidence.says: Fiona Mani completed the PhD dissertation Guns and shikaris at West Virginia University in 2012.

basis: The dissertation is identified, but the sources found do not connect its author to the 2011 review. The shared name and compatible subject alone do not establish identity.

evidence.says: Cites Kathryn A. Abbott's A History of Alcohol as Symbol and Substance in Anishinaabe Culture, a 1996 University of Massachusetts Amherst dissertation.
The 1999 program lists Kathryn Abbott of Western Kentucky University presenting Moving Away from Alcohol: Alcohol and Diaspora among Nineteenth-Century Anishinabeg.

basis: The dissertation and conference paper have a closely related subject, and the conference affiliation matches the review credit. No source found directly connects the dissertation author to that affiliation or to a review, so the topic alone does not establish identity.

evidence.says: Cites Russell Lindley Blake's Ties of Intimacy as a 1978 University of Michigan PhD dissertation.
Identifies Russell Blake as a Ripon College professor since 1981.

basis: The dissertation author and Ripon professor have compatible careers, but the sources found do not connect the dissertation or its author to the reviewer's institution. Shared name and subject alone do not establish identity.

evidence.says: Lists Thomas Knight's Black Towns in Oklahoma as a 1975 PhD dissertation at Oklahoma State University.
Catalogues The Establishment of German Military Government in Belgium, 1940-1941 as a 1967 dissertation, indexed as a doctoral thesis.

basis: The keys represent two distinct doctoral dissertations, dated eight years apart. The second catalogue does not name the author in the displayed record, so the attribution to Knight relies on the supplied graph record; the separation is inferred from the different doctorates.

evidence.says: Lists David Singer's dissertation study of Ludwig Lewisohn at Brown in history and identifies him as a professor at Spertus College.
Lists David G. Singer's The United States Confronts the Soviet Union as a Loyola University Chicago PhD dissertation, awarded in 1972.

basis: The records point to separate history doctorates at Brown and Loyola Chicago, on different dissertations within a few years. The distinction is inferred from those degree records rather than an explicit statement comparing the two scholars.

evidence.says: Susan Splinter authored Gutachten, Experimentalunterricht und Aufklärung, published in 2021.
H-Net credits Susan Splinter with a January 2007 review of Die DDR im Bild.
Susan Splinter's university profile lists her 2001–2006 doctoral work at Halle and her work for Neue Deutsche Biographie from 2011.

basis: The sources identify the authors of each work, but do not establish that the reviewer and the article author are the same person. The shared name and compatible chronology alone are insufficient.

evidence.says: Klaus Becker wrote Stadtkultur und Gesellschaftspolitik, based on his dissertation; he studied in Gießen and Bordeaux from 1991 to his Magister degree in 1997.
Klaus J. Becker reviewed Widerstand, Repression und Verfolgung for H-Soz-Kult in 2015.
Klaus J. Becker, M.A., was researching his Mannheim dissertation Die KPD in Rheinland-Pfalz in 1993–94.

basis: The book author was studying for his first Magister degree through 1997, while the reviewer was already an M.A. conducting research for a different Mannheim dissertation in 1993–94. The overlapping degree trajectories indicate different scholars.

evidence.says: Thomas J. Conroy edited Constructing America's War Culture and was a professor of communication at Castleton State College.
Thomas Conroy, communication chair and co-editor of Constructing America's War Culture, had worked at Castleton for 16 years.
Thomas E. Conroy's 2006 article on Bulfinch cites his dissertation, The Politics of Style: Building, Builders, and the Creation of Federal Boston.
The author of the 2006 Bulfinch article was a visiting history professor at Stonehill College from 2003 to 2007.

basis: The book editor had a long-running Castleton communication career, while the historian associated with the closely matching Boston dissertation held a concurrent history appointment at Stonehill. The dissertation title in the article differs from the queue title, so the identification of the second career is inferred.

evidence.says: The publisher identifies Frances DeBra Brown as the author of An Army in Skirts and describes her as a teacher, artist, and art conservator.

basis: The publisher identifies the book's author, but the sources found do not connect her to the 1975 dissertation or establish a different identity for its author. The shared name alone is insufficient to merge the keys.

evidence.says: Kyle Edmund Harvey authored Prepositional Geographies, a 2019 Cornell history PhD dissertation.
The dissertation's biographical sketch says Harvey began Cornell's history doctoral program in 2012, earning an MA in 2015 and PhD in 2019.
The 2017 article identifies its author Kyle Harvey as a University of Melbourne research fellow and author of American Anti-Nuclear Activism.
The 2014 book American Anti-Nuclear Activism identifies Kyle Harvey as based at Macquarie University.

basis: The dissertation author's Cornell doctoral career from 2012 to 2019 overlaps the anti-nuclear author's established Australian research career, including a 2017 Melbourne fellowship. These are distinct concurrent careers; the conclusion is inferred from the dated institutional evidence.

evidence.says: Stephen Griffin is the author of ‘Duke Leopold of Lorraine, Small State Diplomacy, and the Stuart Court in Exile, 1716–1729’.
Stephen Griffin, coauthor of ‘Irlandois de Nation’, was a PhD candidate at the University of Limerick.

basis: The sources identify the author of the Lorraine scholarship, but do not connect him to Stephen E. Griffin's Washington & Napoleon. The available evidence does not establish whether the two keys represent the same person.

evidence.says: Duane C. Anderson, Iowa state archaeologist, co-authored The Cherokee Excavations.
Iowa state archaeologist Duane Anderson earned a 1972 anthropology PhD at Colorado and directed Iowa museums from 1966 to 1975.
The bibliography cites Duane Charles Anderson's English Working-Class Internationalism as a 1976 University of Oklahoma PhD thesis.

basis: The Cherokee Excavations author had a 1972 Colorado anthropology doctorate and an Iowa museum career, while the other key's history dissertation was a 1976 Oklahoma doctorate. The separate doctorates and overlapping careers strongly indicate two scholars despite their matching names.

evidence.says: Lists Christopher Bailey of Central Michigan University as an author of Private banks in early Michigan, 1837–1884.
Christopher Allen Bailey earned a Texas A&M economics PhD in 2001 and was a Central Michigan economics professor from 2000 to 2021.
Lists Christopher Roderick Bailey as author of the 2004 Edinburgh PhD thesis on SOE and wartime resistance in Albania and Kosovo.
Lists Christopher Roderick Bailey, Edinburgh PhD, as Oxford lecturer in the history of medicine from 2016 to 2018.

basis: The banking article's Central Michigan author matches Christopher Allen Bailey's economics career and 2001 Texas A&M doctorate. The thesis author Christopher Roderick Bailey had an Edinburgh doctorate and an overlapping Oxford appointment, supporting two distinct careers.

evidence.says: Cambridge credits Matthew Vaz with the 2021 article and links the author to ORCID 0000-0002-0084-7522.
A citation identifies The Jackpot Mentality as Matthew Vaz's 2011 Columbia University PhD thesis.
City College identifies its historian Matthew Vaz as holding a Columbia University PhD.

basis: The thesis and the City College historian share a Columbia doctorate, but the article page does not establish that its author is the City College historian. No source found directly connects the article author to the thesis or doctorate.

evidence.says: The Science of Talismans Today identifies Benjamin Anderson with Cornell and ORCID 0000-0002-0392-2997.
Benjamin Anderson was an Edinburgh PhD candidate and tutor in 2022, working on Loyalism in Vermont and the Northern Borderland.
Cornell's Benjamin Anderson is an associate professor in art history and classics with a PhD from Bryn Mawr College.

basis: The Edinburgh reviewer corresponds to an Edinburgh doctoral candidate and tutor in 2022, while the author identified by the other key's ORCID was a Cornell art history and classics professor with a Bryn Mawr PhD. These overlapping, distinct careers support two people.

evidence.says: Christine D. Schmidt's Sühne oder Sanktion? is a revised dissertation accepted at the University of Münster in 2008.
Christine E. Schmidt lists the 2007 H-German review of Architects of Annihilation.
Christine E. Schmidt reports a 2003 PhD from Clark University and work at the Jewish Foundation for the Righteous.

basis: The book author and the reviewer have different middle initials and distinct doctorates and careers. The reviewer's own publications list identifies the specific review and her biography identifies her Clark doctorate; the book derives from a 2008 Münster dissertation.

evidence.says: Christopher Brooke, professor of modern European political thought, holds a Harvard PhD and lists ‘Robert Malthus, Rousseauist’.
Christopher Nugent Lawrence Brooke was a Cambridge medieval historian and professor who did not need a PhD for his career; he died in 2015.
Robert Brentano identifies Christopher Brooke at Cambridge as a reviewer of A New World in a Small Place.
Christopher Brooke reviewed Religious and Laity in Western Europe in 2007.

basis: The Malthus article belongs to a Harvard PhD and Cambridge political theorist, whereas the Cambridge medieval historian died in 2015 and had a different career. Key a is mixed: its Rieti review is also attributed to Christopher Brooke at Cambridge, so the medieval review credits should be examined before any merge or split.

evidence.says: Klaus Gietinger wrote the 2014 review of Konrad's Waldemar Pabst 1880–1970 and cites Klaus Gietinger's Der Konterrevolutionär (2009) in a footnote.
Klaus Gietinger's publication list includes Der Konterrevolutionär: Waldemar Pabst – eine deutsche Karriere (2009).

basis: The review cites the book by a namesake, but does not explicitly identify it as the reviewer's own work. The sources found do not independently establish that the two credits belong to one person.

evidence.says: Lists Harald Haury as author of Von Riesa nach Schloss Elmau (2005).

basis: The book author is confirmed, but I found no source connecting him to the reviewer of Zwischen Sonne und Halbmond or establishing a shared institutional affiliation in the relevant years. The shared name alone does not establish identity.

evidence.says: Monika Kubrova, Halle/S., wrote the 2005 report on Arenen der Elitenvergesellschaftung.
Monika Kubrova's Vom guten Leben was published in 2011 and was also a 2009 dissertation at the University of Halle.

basis: The report identifies its author with Halle, and the book originated as a dissertation at the university there. The report does not identify an institutional affiliation, and the sources do not directly connect the two works to one person.
